title: Abbreviations and acronyms
subtitle: BBC, NATO, satnav, RSVP
summary: Recognise and use the short forms English speakers use every day, from letter-by-letter abbreviations like ATM to acronyms like NATO and clippings like uni.

lesson.heading: Abbreviations for organisations
rows: Central Intelligence Agency - the US agency that collects information about other countries
Military Intelligence 6 - the UK equivalent of the CIA
lesson.note: These are pronounced letter by letter. When the abbreviation is a stressed word in the sentence, the stress falls on the last letter: She works for the **CIA**. I heard it on the **BBC**.

lesson.heading: Other letter-by-letter abbreviations
rows: identity - an identity card or passport
deoxyribonucleic acid, the chemical at the centre of living cells
I owe you - a note promising to pay money back
automated teller machine, the cash machine outside a bank

lesson.heading: Acronyms: abbreviations pronounced as words
lesson.text: An abbreviation that we say as a single word is called an **acronym**. **NATO** is the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and your **PIN** is your Personal Identity Number for a bank or credit card.

examples.text: You won't be able to use the ATM if you've forgotten your **PIN**.

examples.note: SAD = seasonal affective disorder: lacking energy and enthusiasm in winter, where there is little sunlight

examples.text: I don't know where John can be - he's gone **AWOL**.
examples.note: AWOL = absent without leave, i.e. without permission; usually a military expression

lesson.note: Some acronyms feel so much like ordinary words that we no longer write them in capitals: **laser**, **radar**, **scuba**, **sonar**.

lesson.heading: Written abbreviations
rows: at the bottom of a page or form
at the end of a message, when you want to add something
at the end of an invitation
on a headstone where someone is buried

lesson.text: Say each letter for **BBC**, **ATM** and **ID**, but say **NATO**, **PIN** and **AWOL** as ordinary words. If you can pronounce it as a word, English speakers usually do.

exercises.prompt: Please could you buy me a ___ of apples?
exercises.explanation: Kilo is the everyday clipping of kilogram.

exercises.prompt: William Barclay ___ James Stubbs has been charged with burglary.
exercises.explanation: AKA = also known as, used before a second name someone uses.

exercises.prompt: The surgeons used ___ technology to carry out the operation.
exercises.hint: (an acronym now written as an ordinary word)
exercises.explanation: Laser began life as an acronym but is now written as a normal word.

exercises.prompt: My sister works in a very ___ office using all the most up-to-date hardware and software.
exercises.explanation: High-tech is the short form of high-technology.

exercises.prompt: When you're driving it's much easier to use a ___ rather than a road atlas.
exercises.explanation: Satnav is the everyday short form of satellite navigation system.

exercises.prompt: Bats cannot see well and use a kind of ___ to find their way around.
exercises.explanation: Sonar uses sound waves to locate objects; radar uses radio waves.

exercises.prompt: Sort these abbreviations by the area they belong to.
An invitation says: 'Party at Sam and Beth's house, Saturday 14 August, 8 till late. ___ by 28 July.' Which abbreviation goes in the gap?
exercises.explanation: RSVP at the end of an invitation asks you to reply.

exercises.prompt: A note reads: 'I've gone shopping with Ana. Back around six. See you later. Emma. ___ Tom phoned for you.' Which abbreviation goes in the gap?
exercises.explanation: PS (post script) introduces something added after the end of a message.

exercises.prompt: A headstone reads: 'In loving memory of James Goodman, 1945 - 2015. ___'. Which abbreviation goes in the gap?
exercises.explanation: RIP = rest in peace, written where someone is buried.

exercises.statement: At the bottom of a form you see PTO. It means you should turn to the next page.
WHO is the abbreviation for the World Heritage Organisation.
exercises.explanation: WHO stands for the World Health Organisation.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a request.
exercises.answer: Could you send me the figures ASAP?
exercises.explanation: ASAP = as soon as possible, and is said letter by letter.
